lead: At Ephesus Paul meets about twelve disciples who have received only John’s baptism and have not even heard of the Holy Spirit. They are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes. In the Gospel the disciples say they now believe, and Jesus warns them that they will be scattered, yet he is not alone, and he has conquered the world. Psalm 68 sings of God who rises and scatters his enemies, father of orphans and protector of widows.

r.h: Did you receive the Holy Spirit?
set: Paul reaches Ephesus, the great city of the province of Asia, on his third journey, as he had promised (18:21). He will stay there more than two years (19:10). Apollos has meanwhile gone to Corinth (19:1), after Priscilla and Aquila taught him the Way more accurately (18:26). The disciples Paul now finds seem to be in a situation like that of Apollos before he was taught.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul meets disciples and asks about the Holy Spirit.
vv. 3–4: John’s baptism of repentance pointed to Jesus.
vv. 5–7: baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus, the laying on of hands, and the gift of the Spirit.
v. 8: three months of bold preaching in the synagogue about the kingdom of God.
kw: Luke calls them disciples, but they seem to have been followers of John the Baptist’s teaching who had not yet received Christian baptism.
John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance that pointed ahead to “the one who was to come” (v. 4). Christian baptism is baptism into Christ, with the gift of the Spirit.
when Paul had laid his hands
The same gesture by which Peter and John gave the Spirit to the baptized of Samaria (8:14–17). The laying on of hands is the ancient gesture of the gift of the Spirit.
vv: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” They replied, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
They probably knew that John spoke of one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:16). What they had not heard is that the Spirit had now been given.
John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.
Paul does not belittle John. John’s whole work pointed to Jesus. To follow John faithfully is to come to Christ.
When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied

This little Pentecost at Ephesus matches the Pentecost at Jerusalem (2:4), the gift at Samaria (8:17) and at Caesarea (10:44–46). In every place the same Spirit is given to the one Church. The “about twelve” may hint at a new beginning, like the twelve tribes and the Twelve.
ch: The Catechism, explaining the sacrament of Confirmation, recalls that the apostles imparted the gift of the Spirit to the newly baptized by the laying on of hands, and cites this passage (CCC 1288). It is one root of the Church’s practice of Confirmation, in which the bishop, successor of the apostles, lays hands on the candidates and anoints them with chrism. Baptism and Confirmation belong together as sacraments of Christian initiation, completed by the Eucharist.

r.h: Take courage; I have conquered the world
set: These are the last words of the farewell discourse before Jesus’ great prayer to the Father in chapter 17. The disciples think they have understood at last. Jesus loves them, but he knows that in a few hours they will run away.
str: vv. 29–30: the disciples: now you speak plainly; now we believe.
vv. 31–32: Jesus: do you now believe? You will be scattered, but I am not alone.
v. 33: peace in me, persecution in the world, and victory.
kw: The NRSV has “persecution”. The word means pressure, affliction of every kind. Jesus does not promise his disciples a world without trouble.
A word Jesus speaks in the Gospels to the paralysed man, to the woman with the haemorrhage, and to the disciples on the sea: “Take heart, it is I” (Matthew 14:27). Courage comes from his presence.
A perfect tense: the victory is won and remains. John’s first letter echoes it: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5:4).
vv: Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?
Not a rebuke, but a gentle warning. Their faith is real but still untested. It will be tested tonight.
you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.

Jesus is not left without the Father even in the hour of desertion. The cry on the Cross in Matthew and Mark, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, is the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that ends in trust and praise.
In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!
The last word of the discourse. The world in John means the world that refuses God, not the world God loves (3:16). His victory is won on the Cross, which looks like defeat.
ch: The Church hears these words above all when Christians suffer for their faith. Many Christians in many lands live this verse today; we pray for them and for those who wrong them. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, “like a stranger in a foreign land”, presses forward amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God (Lumen Gentium 8, quoting St Augustine). Christ’s peace is not the absence of trouble but his presence in the midst of it.

qa: Why were these disciples baptized again, when the Church does not repeat baptism?

They had not received Christian baptism at all, only John’s baptism of repentance. John’s baptism was not the sacrament of baptism into Christ. Christian baptism, once validly received, is never repeated, because it marks the soul with an indelible spiritual sign (CCC 1272).
study: The disciples at Ephesus had not even heard of the Holy Spirit. How often do I think of the Spirit, and what gift of the Spirit do I most need now?
Jesus says, “Take courage; I have conquered the world.” Which trouble in my life do I need to place under his victory?
